title: The One Question That Instantly Improves Any Team Discussion
author: Colette Molteni
summary: Molteni argues that a single empathic question can break a stalled team discussion: What challenges are you trying to shine a light on? She first diagnoses why meetings loop, noting that But that is how we have always done it is a statement of fear and that leaders must act as catalysts for change by learning what problem people were solving. She then offers tactics for getting a team talking, such as asking colleagues to walk her through a process step by step, and redirecting tension with a parking-lot note and a light, positive turn. A dashboard-review anecdote shows the question drawing out a stakeholder's real need rather than their old steps. The tone is chatty and anecdotal, with some filler.
points: Resistance to change is often fear of the unknown, so find out what problem the old way was solving before proposing a new one.
Asking someone to walk you through a process step by step opens dialogue without implying criticism.
Parking a heated point and shifting to good news can lower the temperature, provided the timing is right.
The question What challenges are you trying to shine a light on? surfaces needs rather than process steps and puts attention on the other person.
In her dashboard review, the stakeholders' explanation of the why exposed a gap the new methodology had missed.
quotes: In Emotional Intelligence by Daniel Goleman, he says, "Being able to put aside one's self-centered focus and impulses has social benefits: it opens the way to empathy, to real listening, to taking another person's perspective.

Change is hard. Whether you are the store clerk, sales rep, or technical person "selling" your new feature, you have to act as an empathy catalyst. To be a catalyst for change, you have to understand their perspective.

The statement, "But that's how we've always done it," is a statement of fear. Fear of the unknown. Fear that they will not be able to solve the problem they have successfully solved in a tried and accurate fashion.
After a pause, you can gently segway through and say, "So, let's put that in the parking lot to address #. On a fun note, does anyone have some good news or wins to share?

The team referred to the HOW behind how they used to get their data but not the NEED. They referred to the steps in their old system, but the piece missing was the WHY. So I asked the big question. We kicked into our empathic listening as a data team. Our stakeholders immediately explained the WHY. It was to track contract status for follow-up, usually around the third week of the month. This would enable revenue generation before the close of the month. In this explanation, there was no mention of the steps in the old system; it was just the need.
Whether you are resisting change, unlocking a more positive and forward-moving conversation, or just needing to ask an intelligent question, keep this one in your back pocket.
